title: Product Differentiation and Market Segmentation as Alternative Marketing Strategies
author_source: Smith, W. R., Journal of Marketing 21(1), 3-8, 1956, article
note: The founding text of segmentation (approx. 1,900 citations): frames segmentation as adjusting the product and marketing mix to heterogeneous demand ('bending supply to demand') versus differentiation ('bending demand to supply'). Only 6 pages, which makes it ideal for close reading of the original definition.
course_use: Core reading for session 1; contrast with Dickson & Ginter (1987). Paid (SAGE); WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: New Criteria for Market Segmentation
author_source: Yankelovich, D., Harvard Business Review 42(2), 83-90, March 1964, article
note: Argues that demographics alone lose predictive power and proposes non-demographic bases (values, tastes, purchase motives, aesthetic preferences) using examples such as watches and cars. It is the origin of the 'non-demographic segmentation' idea, and Yankelovich himself revisited it in 2006.
course_use: Discussion reading paired with Yankelovich & Meer (2006): what changed in 40 years? HBR paid; WU access via EBSCO Business Source, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Benefit Segmentation: A Decision-Oriented Research Tool
author_source: Haley, R. I., Journal of Marketing 32(3), 30-35, 1968, article
note: The classic toothpaste example segments buyers by benefit sought (Sensory, Sociable, Worrier, Independent segments) and profiles each by demographics, behaviour and personality. It is the clearest worked illustration of benefits as the causal base and descriptors as profile variables.
course_use: Reading plus in-class exercise: students build a benefit-segment table for a local product (e.g. banking app). Paid (SAGE); WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Benefit Segmentation - 20 Years Later
author_source: Haley, R. I., Journal of Consumer Marketing 1(2), 5-13, 1984, article
note: Haley reflects on two decades of applying benefit segmentation: what worked, how the method evolved, and practical lessons on implementing segments in product and advertising decisions.
course_use: Optional follow-up to Haley (1968) to show how practice evolves. Emerald; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Concept and Application of Life Style Segmentation
author_source: Plummer, J. T., Journal of Marketing 38(1), 33-37, 1974, article
note: Introduces AIO (activities, interests, opinions) lifestyle segmentation and shows how lifestyle profiles of heavy users inform creative strategy. A short foundational text for psychographic segmentation bases.
course_use: Background reading for the psychographics/lifestyle unit; pair with Wells (1975) critique. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Psychographics: A Critical Review
author_source: Wells, W. D., Journal of Marketing Research 12(2), 196-213, 1975, article
note: Reviews early psychographic research and assesses its reliability, validity and usefulness, distinguishing lifestyle profiles, product-specific profiles and general typologies. Useful for teaching that psychographic bases need validation evidence.
course_use: Background or seminar reading on psychographic bases and their measurement problems. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Alternative Measurement Approaches to Consumer Values: The List of Values (LOV) and Values and Life Style (VALS)
author_source: Kahle, L. R., Beatty, S. E., Homer, P., Journal of Consumer Research 13(3), 405-409, 1986, article
note: A short empirical comparison of the proprietary VALS typology with the public-domain List of Values. LOV predicted consumer-behaviour trends at least as well as VALS. Good evidence for a discussion of commercial lifestyle typologies (VALS, Sinus-Milieus) versus open measures.
course_use: Short reading for the values/lifestyle segmentation session; link to Strategic Business Insights' VALS survey demo. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Value-System Segmentation: Exploring the Meaning of LOV
author_source: Kamakura, W. A., Novak, T. P., Journal of Consumer Research 19(1), 119-132, 1992, article
note: Segments consumers by value systems, meaning the ranking of the Rokeach/LOV values, with a latent-class ranking model. It bridges values-based segmentation and latent class methods.
course_use: Advanced reading for students interested in values-based segmentation; links to the latent class methods row. WU-Lizenz prüfen; SSRN version available

title: Issues and Advances in Segmentation Research
author_source: Wind, Y., Journal of Marketing Research 15(3), 317-337, 1978, article
note: The canonical state-of-the-art review. It distinguishes a-priori from post-hoc (clustering-based) segmentation designs, reviews bases and methods, and sets a research agenda. Its a-priori vs post-hoc typology still structures methods teaching.
course_use: Key reading for the methods unit; use its a-priori vs post-hoc typology as a lecture framework. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Industrial Market Segmentation
author_source: Wind, Y., Cardozo, R. N., Industrial Marketing Management 3(3), 153-165, 1974, article
note: Proposes the two-stage B2B approach: macro-segmentation (organisational characteristics such as industry, size, end use) followed by micro-segmentation (decision-making unit characteristics). This is the predecessor to the Bonoma & Shapiro nested model.
course_use: Reading for the B2B session; compare two-stage vs nested approaches. Elsevier; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: How to Segment Industrial Markets
author_source: Shapiro, B. P., Bonoma, T. V., Harvard Business Review 62(3), 104-110, May 1984, article (based on Bonoma & Shapiro, Segmenting the Industrial Market, Lexington Books, 1983)
note: The nested approach: five layers from outer to inner (demographics, operating variables, purchasing approaches, situational factors, personal characteristics of buyers). Outer layers are cheap to observe, inner layers costly but more actionable. The standard B2B segmentation framework in textbooks.
course_use: Core B2B reading plus exercise: apply the nested 'onion' to a B2B firm (e.g. an Austrian industrial supplier). HBR paid; WU access via EBSCO, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: B2B Market Segmentation: A Systematic Review and Research Agenda
author_source: Mora Cortez, R., Clarke, A. H., Freytag, P. V., Journal of Business Research 126, 415-428, 2021, article
note: A systematic review of B2B segmentation research since the 1970s. It maps bases, processes and implementation themes and shows how the field moved from Wind & Cardozo and Bonoma & Shapiro to value- and relationship-based segmentation. An up-to-date bridge to the classics.
course_use: Background or reading for the B2B session; the accepted manuscript is open access in the SDU repository (findresearcher.sdu.dk). Elsevier version: WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Market Segmentation, Product Differentiation, and Marketing Strategy
author_source: Dickson, P. R., Ginter, J. L., Journal of Marketing 51(2), 1-10, 1987, article
note: Corrects the widespread misreading of Smith (1956): segmentation and product differentiation are complementary rather than alternative strategies. Introduces demand-function modification and the perceptual/benefit-space view, which link segmentation directly to positioning.
course_use: Core reading to connect S to P in STP; good for a debate 'segmentation vs differentiation'. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Market Segmentation: A Review
author_source: Beane, T. P., Ennis, D. M., European Journal of Marketing 21(5), 20-42, 1987, article
note: A readable review of consumer segmentation bases (geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioural/benefit) and techniques, with a decision-oriented view of choosing bases. A good student-level overview article.
course_use: Accessible background reading for undergraduates. Emerald; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Simultaneous Approach to Market Segmentation and Market Structuring
author_source: Grover, R., Srinivasan, V., Journal of Marketing Research 24(2), 139-153, 1987, article
note: Uses a latent class model on brand-switching panel data to identify segments and competitive market structure simultaneously (brand-loyal vs switching segments). A classic link between segmentation and competitive analysis, and therefore to positioning.
course_use: Advanced reading for MSc/analytics track; shows segmentation from scanner data. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Probabilistic Choice Model for Market Segmentation and Elasticity Structure
author_source: Kamakura, W. A., Russell, G. J., Journal of Marketing Research 26(4), 379-390, 1989, article
note: The landmark latent class (finite mixture) multinomial logit model. It identifies segments that differ in price sensitivity and brand preference from household purchase data (approx. 1,300 citations). The foundation of response-based segmentation.
course_use: Advanced methods reading; pair with the latent class/finite mixture methods row and an R flexmix lab. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Segmenting Markets with Conjoint Analysis
author_source: Green, P. E., Krieger, A. M., Journal of Marketing 55(4), 20-31, 1991, article
note: Shows how to segment on conjoint part-worths (benefit/needs-based segmentation) and compares a-priori, post-hoc clustering and componential approaches. It links segmentation to product design and positioning simulations.
course_use: Reading for a needs-based segmentation session; supports a conjoint-plus-clustering lab. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Market Segmentation: Conceptual and Methodological Foundations (2nd ed.)
author_source: Wedel, M., Kamakura, W. A., Kluwer/Springer, International Series in Quantitative Marketing, 2000, book
note: The standard reference monograph. It classifies bases (observable/unobservable x general/product-specific), sets six segment-effectiveness criteria (identifiability, substantiality, accessibility, stability, responsiveness, actionability), and covers clustering, mixture and mixture-regression models in depth. Use the Ch. 1-2 tables as lecture slides.
course_use: Instructor background; selected chapters (1-2 bases and criteria) for MSc students. SpringerLink: WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Marketing Models of Consumer Heterogeneity
author_source: Allenby, G. M., Rossi, P. E., Journal of Econometrics 89(1-2), 57-78, 1998, article
note: Contrasts discrete segment (finite mixture) representations of heterogeneity with continuous hierarchical Bayes models and shows the value of individual-level estimates for targeting. Conceptual grounding for the shift from segments to a 'segment of one'.
course_use: Advanced background for analytics-oriented students; discussion: are segments real or a convenient approximation? Elsevier; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: International Market Segmentation: Issues and Perspectives
author_source: Steenkamp, J.-B. E. M., ter Hofstede, F., International Journal of Research in Marketing 19(3), 185-213, 2002, article
note: Reviews cross-national segmentation: country-level vs consumer-level segments, measurement invariance, and cross-border segments. Highly relevant for European/CEE marketing contexts at WU.
course_use: Reading for an international segmentation session; case discussion on pan-European segments. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Market Segmentation: Diagnosing and Treating the Barriers
author_source: Dibb, S., Simkin, L., Industrial Marketing Management 30(8), 609-625, 2001, article
note: Identifies implementation barriers before, during and after a segmentation exercise (infrastructure, process, implementation) and proposes diagnostic treatments from case evidence. The key text explaining why many segmentation projects fail in organisations.
course_use: Core reading for the implementation session; students diagnose barriers in a case company. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Evaluating Market-Segmentation Research Priorities: Targeting Re-emancipation
author_source: Quinn, L., Dibb, S., Journal of Marketing Management 26(13-14), 1239-1255, 2010, article
note: Argues that segmentation research neglected targeting and implementation in favour of technique. It calls for refocusing on how segments are selected and used, which helps move the class from 'S' to 'T'.
course_use: Seminar discussion reading on the theory-practice gap. Taylor & Francis; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Market Segmentation in Practice: Review of Empirical Studies, Methodological Assessment, and Agenda for Future Research
author_source: Foedermayr, E. K., Diamantopoulos, A., Journal of Strategic Marketing 16(3), 223-265, 2008, article
note: Reviews empirical studies of how firms actually segment (bases used, process, problems) and assesses their methods. Co-authored at the University of Vienna. Good evidence of the gap between textbook STP and company practice.
course_use: Background reading; use the findings tables for a lecture slide on segmentation in practice. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Marktsegmentierung in der Unternehmenspraxis - Stellenwert, Vorgehen und Herausforderungen
author_source: Kesting, T., Nufer, G., Rennhak, C., Reutlinger Diskussionsbeiträge zu Marketing & Management No. 2007-2, 2007, working paper (German)
note: A German-language survey of segmentation practice in German companies: a large gap between methods known in theory and those used, with use driven by firm size, industry and business area, and the most untapped potential in SMEs and retail. A short, free German source for practice-oriented discussion.
course_use: Optional German reading or source for a practice-gap discussion. Free PDF in the Tübingen repository

title: Markt- und Kundensegmentierung: Kundenorientierte Markterfassung und -bearbeitung (2. Aufl.)
author_source: Freter, H., Kohlhammer, Stuttgart, 2008, book (German)
note: The standard German textbook on segmentation. Covers segmentation criteria (including value-oriented customer segmentation), segment selection, segment-specific marketing and an introductory overview of multivariate methods for segment identification. Useful for German terminology (Marktsegmentierung, Marktbearbeitung, Kundenwert).
course_use: German reference text for students writing seminar or Bachelor theses; check the WU library holdings. Paid print book

title: Rediscovering Market Segmentation
author_source: Yankelovich, D., Meer, D., Harvard Business Review 84(2), 122-131, February 2006, article
note: Argues that psychographic profiling has become a wasteful detour from segmentation's real purpose: finding customers whose behaviour can be changed or whose needs are unmet. Introduces the 'gravity of decision spectrum' to choose bases according to how much a purchase matters to the consumer. Cites a survey in which 59% of firms ran a major segmentation study but only 14% saw real value.
course_use: Core discussion reading on managerial relevance; pair with Yankelovich (1964). HBR paid; WU access via EBSCO, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Marketing Malpractice: The Cause and the Cure
author_source: Christensen, C. M., Cook, S., Hall, T., Harvard Business Review 83(12), 74-83, December 2005, article
note: A jobs-to-be-done critique of segmentation by product category and customer demographics, written against a backdrop of 30,000 launches a year and a failure rate above 90%. Includes the milkshake example (commuters 'hire' a milkshake for a boring drive) and argues for segmenting by the circumstance or job instead.
course_use: Discussion or debate reading: demographic/psychographic vs job-based segmentation; works well with a short in-class 'milkshake' exercise. HBR paid; WU via EBSCO, WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Know Your Customers' 'Jobs to Be Done'
author_source: Christensen, C. M., Hall, T., Dillon, K., Duncan, D. S., Harvard Business Review 94(9), 54-62, September 2016, article
note: An updated jobs-to-be-done statement with examples (e.g. Southern New Hampshire University, IKEA). It explains functional, social and emotional dimensions of a job and how they replace correlation-based customer profiles. A useful practitioner complement to the 2005 critique.
course_use: Optional reading or pre-class video tie-in; supports a JTBD-segment canvas exercise. HBR paid; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Market Segmentation for Competitive Brands
author_source: Hammond, K., Ehrenberg, A. S. C., Goodhardt, G. J., European Journal of Marketing 30(12), 39-49, 1996, article
note: Ehrenberg-Bass evidence that competing brands in a category sell to customers with very similar demographic and attitudinal profiles, so brand-level segmentation is rarely found and markets are largely unsegmented between direct competitors. The empirical core of the 'sophisticated mass marketing' critique (Sharp, How Brands Grow).
course_use: Core counter-reading for a debate 'Is segmentation dead?'; contrast with Smith (1956) and Dickson & Ginter. Emerald; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: In 25 Years, Across 50 Categories, User Profiles for Directly Competing Brands Seldom Differ
author_source: Uncles, M. D., Kennedy, R., Nenycz-Thiel, M., Singh, J., Kwok, S., Journal of Advertising Research 52(2), 252-261, 2012, article
note: A large-scale replication across 50 categories and 25 years: user profiles of directly competing brands rarely differ on demographics, so brands compete for the same buyers. Strong empirical data for discussing the limits of targeting and the case for broad reach.
course_use: Reading or data example for the Ehrenberg-Bass critique; students can predict and then check brand-profile differences. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Review of Data-Driven Market Segmentation in Tourism
author_source: Dolnicar, S., Journal of Travel & Tourism Marketing 12(1), 1-22, 2002, article
note: Audits 47 published data-driven segmentation studies and documents recurring methodological flaws: too many variables for the sample size, arbitrary choice of the number of clusters, no stability checks, and factor-cluster segmentation. A checklist of what not to do.
course_use: Reading for the methods-critique session; students use its criteria to audit a published segmentation study. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Methodological Reasons for the Theory/Practice Divide in Market Segmentation
author_source: Dolnicar, S., Lazarevski, K., Journal of Marketing Management 25(3-4), 357-373, 2009, article
note: A survey of marketing managers showing that many do not understand data-driven segmentation outputs, see segments as given rather than constructed, and rarely question the analyst's choices. Explains why segmentation results are misused and links method choices to managerial trust.
course_use: Discussion reading on the manager-analyst interface; pairs with Dibb & Simkin (2001). WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Market Segmentation Analysis: Understanding It, Doing It, and Making It Useful
author_source: Sara Dolnicar, Bettina Grün, Friedrich Leisch; Springer Singapore (Management for Professionals), 2018; monograph, CC BY 4.0
note: Best free STP methods book: a ten-step segmentation process (deciding (not) to segment, specifying the ideal target segment, collecting and exploring data, extracting segments with k-means/hierarchical/mixture models, profiling, describing, selecting target segment(s), customising the marketing mix, evaluation and monitoring) with checklists per step; R code and datasets (R package MSA) to replicate everything. Co-authors: Dolnicar (WU alumna, now UQ), Grün (now Universität Innsbruck, formerly WU), the late Leisch (BOKU Vienna).
course_use: Assign step chapters as hands-on lab readings; full PDF free via SpringerLink/OAPEN - open access.

title: Required Sample Sizes for Data-Driven Market Segmentation Analyses in Tourism
author_source: Dolnicar, S., Grün, B., Leisch, F., Schmidt, K., Journal of Travel Research 53(3), 296-306, 2014, article
note: A simulation study giving the rule of thumb that data-driven segmentation needs at least 70 times the number of segmentation variables (e.g. 20 variables need at least 1,400 respondents). Shows that most published studies are under-powered.
course_use: Short reading for the methods lab; students check whether their own survey data meet the 70x rule. Open access (SAGE)

title: A Survey of the Challenges and Pitfalls of Cluster Analysis Application in Market Segmentation
author_source: Tuma, M. N., Decker, R., Scholz, S. W., International Journal of Market Research 53(3), 391-414, 2011, article
note: Reviews about 200 segmentation studies in marketing journals and documents common pitfalls: data standardisation, variable selection, algorithm choice, number of clusters and missing validation. A good quality-control checklist for student projects.
course_use: Methods reading; turn its findings into a grading rubric for segmentation projects. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Approaches to Customer Segmentation
author_source: Cooil, B., Aksoy, L., Keiningham, T. L., Journal of Relationship Marketing 6(3-4), 9-39, 2008, article
note: A tutorial-style overview of segmentation approaches (a-priori, cluster, latent class, CHAID/tree, CLV-based) with worked examples in a relationship-marketing context. Accessible for business students without a statistics background.
course_use: Background reading bridging concepts and methods for undergraduates. Taylor & Francis; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: The Customer Pyramid: Creating and Serving Profitable Customers
author_source: Zeithaml, V. A., Rust, R. T., Lemon, K. N., California Management Review 43(4), 118-142, 2001, article
note: Profitability-based segmentation into Platinum, Gold, Iron and Lead tiers, with strategies to serve, upgrade or divest each tier. The standard illustration of value/CLV-based segmentation and its ethical side (firing customers).
course_use: Reading plus discussion: is it fair to de-prioritise 'lead' customers? SAGE/CMR; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Customer Lifetime Value Framework for Customer Selection and Resource Allocation Strategy
author_source: Venkatesan, R., Kumar, V., Journal of Marketing 68(4), 106-125, 2004, article
note: Shows in a B2B field setting that selecting customers by predicted CLV outperforms RFM- and past-value-based selection in future profit. Key evidence for CLV-based targeting.
course_use: Reading for the targeting/CLV session; compare RFM vs CLV targeting rules. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Dynamic Segmentation Approach for Targeting and Customizing Direct Marketing Campaigns
author_source: Reutterer, T., Mild, A., Natter, M., Taudes, A., Journal of Interactive Marketing 20(3-4), 43-57, 2006, article
note: A WU Vienna study: purchase-history-based segmentation of a retailer's customer base that updates as behaviour changes, with segment-specific campaign customisation and evaluation of response. A home-grown example of behavioural segmentation linked to targeting.
course_use: Case-style reading for behavioural/database segmentation; invite WU authors as guest speakers. Wiley; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Combined Approach for Segment-Specific Market Basket Analysis
author_source: Boztug, Y., Reutterer, T., European Journal of Operational Research 187(1), 294-312, 2008, article
note: Segments shopping baskets (not customers) by cross-category purchase patterns using a prototype-based clustering approach, then estimates segment-specific cross-category effects. Shows behavioural segmentation of transaction data for retail promotions (WU co-author).
course_use: Advanced reading for retail analytics students; open working-paper version via EconStor (hdl.handle.net/10419/25089). Elsevier: WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Customer Segments as Moving Targets: Integrating Customer Value Dynamism into Segment Instability Logic
author_source: Blocker, C. P., Flint, D. J., Industrial Marketing Management 36(6), 810-822, 2007, article
note: Explains why segments are unstable over time (changing customer value perceptions) and proposes how to monitor and manage segment instability in B2B. Supports teaching the 'stability' criterion.
course_use: Reading for the segment-validity session; discuss how often segments should be refreshed. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Markets of a Single Customer: Exploiting Conceptual Developments in Market Segmentation
author_source: Kara, A., Kaynak, E., European Journal of Marketing 31(11/12), 873-895, 1997, article
note: Traces the evolution from mass marketing to segment, niche and finally 'segment-of-one' marketing, driven by database and flexible-manufacturing technologies. Conceptual anchor for micro-segmentation.
course_use: Background reading for the personalisation/micro-segmentation session. Emerald; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Putting One-to-One Marketing to Work: Personalization, Customization, and Choice
author_source: Arora, N., Dreze, X., Ghose, A., Hess, J. D., et al., Marketing Letters 19(3-4), 305-321, 2008, article
note: Distinguishes firm-initiated personalisation from customer-initiated customisation and reviews the research on when one-to-one marketing pays off. A clear conceptual vocabulary for segment-of-one strategies.
course_use: Reading for the personalisation session; frame a debate on personalisation vs privacy. Springer; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Emerging Segmentation Practices in the Age of the Social Customer
author_source: Canhoto, A. I., Clark, M., Fennemore, P., Journal of Strategic Marketing 21(5), 413-428, 2013, article
note: Case-based study of how firms segment using social-media and digital data: shifting from static profiles to dynamic, behaviour- and context-based segments, plus the organisational challenges this creates.
course_use: Reading for the digital segmentation session. Taylor & Francis; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Crumbs of the Cookie: User Profiling in Customer-Base Analysis and Behavioral Targeting
author_source: Trusov, M., Ma, L., Jamal, Z., Marketing Science 35(3), 405-426, 2016, article
note: Infers latent user profiles (interests/'roles') from browsing cookies with a topic-model approach and shows improved behavioural targeting of display ads. A concrete example of digital behavioural segmentation at scale.
course_use: Advanced reading for the digital/behavioural targeting session; also useful for a third-party-cookie phase-out discussion. INFORMS; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Marketing Analytics for Data-Rich Environments
author_source: Wedel, M., Kannan, P. K., Journal of Marketing 80(6), 97-121, 2016, article
note: A broad review of analytics for big data, covering personalisation, customer-level targeting and the move from segment-level to individual-level models, as well as privacy and data-security constraints. Good bridge from classic segmentation to data-driven personalisation.
course_use: Background reading for the recent-developments session. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Machine Learning and AI in Marketing - Connecting Computing Power to Human Insights
author_source: Ma, L., Sun, B., International Journal of Research in Marketing 37(3), 481-504, 2020, article
note: Reviews ML methods (unsupervised clustering, topic models, deep learning) for marketing problems, including segmentation and targeting, and discusses interpretability vs prediction. A reference point for 'ML segmentation' claims.
course_use: Background reading for the ML segmentation session. Elsevier; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Review on Customer Segmentation Methods for Personalized Customer Targeting in E-Commerce Use Cases
author_source: Alves Gomes, M., Meisen, T., Information Systems and e-Business Management 21(3), 527-570, 2023, article
note: A systematic review of 105 papers (2000-2022) that derives a four-phase process (data collection, customer representation, segmentation, targeting). Finds that RFM and manual feature selection dominate customer representation and that k-means is by far the most used algorithm, regardless of data size.
course_use: Reading for the ML/e-commerce segmentation session; the process figure works as a lecture slide. Open access (Springer, CC BY)

title: Targeting Prospective Customers: Robustness of Machine-Learning Methods to Typical Data Challenges
author_source: Simester, D., Timoshenko, A., Zoumpoulis, S. I., Management Science 66(6), 2495-2522, 2020, article
note: A field-experiment-based comparison of ML targeting models (lasso, random forest, etc.) under realistic data problems (distribution shift, limited data). Shows when sophisticated models fail to beat simpler ones, a useful corrective to ML hype in targeting.
course_use: Advanced reading for analytics students; the author version is open in MIT DSpace (hdl.handle.net/1721.1/130508). INFORMS: WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: A Survey of 15 Years of Data-Driven Persona Development
author_source: Salminen, J., Guan, K., Jung, S.-G., Jansen, B. J., International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction 37(18), 1685-1708, 2021, article
note: Reviews 77 studies that create personas from data (clustering, matrix factorisation, LDA) and discusses validation and the risk of stereotyping. Connects segmentation output to personas as a communication device for implementation.
course_use: Reading or background for a persona workshop: turn cluster solutions into personas. Open access (Taylor & Francis)

title: Revitalizing Segmentation in Strategic Marketing: Introducing a Special Issue Driven by Technological, Empirical, and Methodological Advancements
author_source: Mergner, N., Brüggemann, P., Thaichon, P., Journal of Strategic Marketing (online first), 1-9, 2026, editorial
note: A 2026 editorial arguing that segmentation is far from obsolete despite AI. It summarises special-issue contributions on ML-based segment formation, text-based segmentation and data-quality/validation risks. The most current statement of the debate, with pointers to new papers.
course_use: Short up-to-date reading to close the course unit; check the special issue for further papers. Taylor & Francis; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: k-means clustering (partitioning)
author_source: Hartigan, J. A., Wong, M. A., Algorithm AS 136: A K-Means Clustering Algorithm, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics) 28(1), 100-108, 1979, article
note: The standard k-means algorithm implemented in R's kmeans() (default method). Teaching points: needs a pre-set k and multiple random starts, is sensitive to scaling and outliers, and favours spherical, similar-sized clusters. Gomes & Meisen (2023) show it is the most used method in customer segmentation.
course_use: Lab: k-means on survey or RFM data in R or Python; compare 10 random starts. Paid (JSTOR); WU JSTOR licence

title: Hierarchical agglomerative clustering (Ward's method)
author_source: Ward, J. H., Hierarchical Grouping to Optimize an Objective Function, Journal of the American Statistical Association 58(301), 236-244, 1963, article
note: Ward's minimum-variance linkage, the default hierarchical method in marketing segmentation. Teaching points: the dendrogram shows candidate numbers of clusters, it does not scale to large n, and early merges cannot be undone. Often used to seed k-means (two-stage approach, see Punj & Stewart 1983).
course_use: Lab: dendrogram on a small data set; compare with k-means solution. Taylor & Francis; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Cluster analysis in marketing: choosing algorithms, two-stage Ward + k-means
author_source: Punj, G., Stewart, D. W., Cluster Analysis in Marketing Research: Review and Suggestions for Application, Journal of Marketing Research 20(2), 134-148, 1983, article
note: The most-cited marketing review of cluster analysis (approx. 2,400 citations). It compares algorithms and recommends a two-stage procedure: hierarchical (Ward) to find the number and starting centroids, then k-means to refine. It also covers distance measures and validation.
course_use: Key methods reading before the clustering lab. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Latent class analysis / finite mixture models (model-based segmentation)
author_source: Leisch, F., FlexMix: A General Framework for Finite Mixture Models and Latent Class Regression in R, Journal of Statistical Software 11(8), 2004, article
note: Model-based segmentation that assumes data come from a mixture of segment-specific distributions. It gives probabilistic membership and information criteria (AIC/BIC) for choosing the number of segments, handles mixed data types, and extends to mixture regression (segments that differ in response, as in Kamakura & Russell 1989). Magidson & Vermunt (2002, Canadian Journal of Marketing Research 20) show latent class models outperform k-means in simulation. Theory: Wedel & Kamakura (2000).
course_use: Lab: flexmix in R (used in Dolnicar, Grün & Leisch 2018); compare BIC across 2-8 segments. Free, open access (JSS)

title: RFM (recency, frequency, monetary value) segmentation and its link to CLV
author_source: Fader, P. S., Hardie, B. G. S., Lee, K. L., RFM and CLV: Using Iso-Value Curves for Customer Base Analysis, Journal of Marketing Research 42(4), 415-430, 2005, article
note: Links the practitioner RFM scoring to a formal CLV model (Pareto/NBD + gamma-gamma) and visualises iso-value curves showing which R/F/M combinations have equal future value. Earlier RFM-based direct-mail selection: Bult & Wansbeek (1995), Marketing Science 14(4), 378-394, https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.14.4.378.
course_use: Lab: RFM quintile scoring on the UCI Online Retail data set, then compare with BTYD/CLV predictions (R package BTYD or Python lifetimes). WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: TwoStep clustering for mixed categorical and continuous data (SPSS TwoStep)
author_source: Chiu, T., Fang, D., Chen, J., Wang, Y., Jeris, C., A Robust and Scalable Clustering Algorithm for Mixed Type Attributes in Large Database Environment, Proc. 7th ACM SIGKDD, 263-268, 2001, conference paper
note: The algorithm behind SPSS TwoStep: a pre-clustering CF-tree followed by hierarchical clustering with a log-likelihood distance and automatic BIC-based choice of k. Widely used by students because it handles categorical variables. Teaching point: the automatic k is not a substitute for stability checks.
course_use: Background for students using SPSS; demo TwoStep vs k-means on the same data. ACM; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Factor-cluster segmentation pitfall (clustering on factor scores)
author_source: Dolnicar, S., Grün, B., Challenging 'Factor-Cluster Segmentation', Journal of Travel Research 47(1), 63-71, 2008, article
note: Shows with artificial data that running PCA/factor analysis first and clustering the factor scores can discard the information that separates segments and fail to recover the true structure. Recommends clustering the raw items, or using biclustering or variable selection instead.
course_use: Methods-critique reading; lab: compare clusters on raw items vs factor scores. SAGE; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Determining the number of clusters (elbow/scree, internal indices)
author_source: Milligan, G. W., Cooper, M. C., An Examination of Procedures for Determining the Number of Clusters in a Data Set, Psychometrika 50(2), 159-179, 1985, article
note: A Monte Carlo comparison of 30 stopping rules (Calinski-Harabasz performed best). The basis for multi-index tools such as R NbClust. Teaching point: the elbow plot is a heuristic, so several indices plus managerial interpretability should guide the choice of k.
course_use: Lab: compute elbow, Calinski-Harabasz and gap statistic for k = 2-8. Springer; WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Silhouette coefficient for cluster validation
author_source: Rousseeuw, P. J., Silhouettes: A Graphical Aid to the Interpretation and Validation of Cluster Analysis, Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 20, 53-65, 1987, article
note: Defines the silhouette width per observation (cohesion vs separation, from -1 to 1) and the silhouette plot. The most common internal validity index in student segmentation projects; average silhouette above about 0.5 indicates reasonable structure.
course_use: Lab: silhouette plots in R (cluster::silhouette) or Python (sklearn). Open access (Elsevier archive)

title: Segment stability / reproducibility via bootstrapping
author_source: Dolnicar, S., Leisch, F., Evaluation of Structure and Reproducibility of Cluster Solutions Using the Bootstrap, Marketing Letters 21(1), 83-101, 2010, article
note: Proposes repeated bootstrap clustering and the adjusted Rand index to assess whether segments are natural, reproducible or constructed. This lets students choose k by stability and is a concrete operationalisation of the 'stability' criterion.
course_use: Lab: stability boxplots with R flexclust::bootFlexclust (as in Dolnicar, Grün & Leisch 2018). Open access version via LMU ePub (doi.org/10.5282/ubm/epub.10960)

title: CHAID / decision-tree (a-priori, criterion-based) segmentation
author_source: Kass, G. V., An Exploratory Technique for Investigating Large Quantities of Categorical Data, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series C (Applied Statistics) 29(2), 119-127, 1980, article
note: Introduces CHAID (chi-square automatic interaction detection), which splits customers into segments that differ on a dependent variable (e.g. response, purchase). A supervised alternative to clustering that produces easily communicated rules and is widely used in direct marketing and SPSS.
course_use: Lab: tree-based segmentation of campaign response (R partykit/rpart, SPSS Decision Trees); compare with cluster-based segments. JSTOR; WU JSTOR licence

title: Discriminant analysis for segment profiling and assignment
author_source: Morrison, D. G., On the Interpretation of Discriminant Analysis, Journal of Marketing Research 6(2), 156-163, 1969, article
note: A classic marketing treatment of discriminant analysis: how to interpret functions and classification hit rates against chance criteria. In segmentation it is used after clustering to profile segments with descriptor variables and to assign new customers to segments (with multinomial logit as an alternative).
course_use: Lab: profile cluster segments with LDA or multinomial logit; discuss hit-rate vs chance. WU-Lizenz prüfen

title: Prioritising Target Markets
author_source: Lyndon Simkin & Sally Dibb, Marketing Intelligence & Planning 16(7), 407-417, 1998, article
note: Practitioner-oriented study of how companies choose target segments; lists segment attractiveness criteria (size, growth, profitability, competition, fit with capabilities) and shows a directional-policy/attractiveness-matrix approach to prioritisation.
course_use: Basis for an in-class segment-attractiveness scoring exercise. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Business to Business Market Segmentation
author_source: Per Vagn Freytag & Ann Hojbjerg Clarke, Industrial Marketing Management 30(6), 473-486, 2001, article
note: Develops a model for segment selection in B2B that combines future demand, resource requirements and organisational fit; shows that targeting is a strategic resource-allocation decision, not only a data exercise.
course_use: Use for B2B targeting cases and project work. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Brand User Profiles Seldom Change and Seldom Differ
author_source: Zachary W. Anesbury, Margaret Winchester & Rachel Kennedy, Marketing Letters 28(4), 523-535, 2017, article
note: Shows that brand user profiles are also stable over time, so brands cannot easily move into a new target group; challenges repositioning towards a younger or different audience.
course_use: Use with a repositioning case (e.g. a brand trying to get younger). WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Evidence Concerning the Importance of Perceived Brand Differentiation
author_source: Jenni Romaniuk, Byron Sharp & Andrew Ehrenberg, Australasian Marketing Journal 15(2), 42-54, 2007, article
note: Finds that only a small share of buyers see their brand as different or unique, and this share is similar across competing brands; argues for distinctiveness (brand assets, salience) over perceived differentiation.
course_use: Core reading for the 'differentiation vs distinctiveness' discussion of positioning. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: What is Differentiation and How Does it Work?
author_source: Byron Sharp & John Dawes, Journal of Marketing Management 17(7-8), 739-759, 2001, article
note: Conceptual paper redefining differentiation broadly (any reason buyers choose one brand over another), including salience and availability; bridges Porter-style differentiation and Ehrenberg-Bass thinking.
course_use: Theory reading linking positioning/differentiation to Porter's generic strategies. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Mark Ritson: Ditching targeting for mass marketing is going back to the dark ages
author_source: Mark Ritson, Marketing Week, column, 2016
note: Ritson's rebuttal to the anti-targeting trend (Mars, Ehrenberg-Bass): rejecting targeting also rejects positioning and differentiation. Accessible and polemical; argues for doing both broad reach (cf. Binet & Field, The Long and the Short of It) and targeted activation.
course_use: Pre-class reading for a structured debate 'Is targeting dead?'. Free with Marketing Week registration (limited free articles).

title: Ritson versus Sharp: Who won the clash of the marketing titans?
author_source: Marketing Week, report on the Ritson-Sharp debate at the Festival of Marketing, 2016
note: Summarises both positions on mass marketing vs targeting in one place, including Ritson's 'you can do both' line and Sharp's reach argument; useful as a neutral debate brief.
course_use: Students map each argument to evidence (Uncles et al. 2012 vs Ritson). Marketing Week, registration may be needed.

title: The Value of Purchase History Data in Target Marketing
author_source: Peter E. Rossi, Robert E. McCulloch & Greg M. Allenby, Marketing Science 15(4), 321-340, 1996, article
note: Classic quantification of the value of individual-level data for targeted couponing: purchase history raises the value of targeting substantially over demographics alone. Shows how to value information for micro-targeting.
course_use: Advanced/quantitative session on micro-targeting and data value. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Privacy Regulation and Online Advertising
author_source: Avi Goldfarb & Catherine E. Tucker, Management Science 57(1), 57-71, 2011, article
note: Uses the EU e-Privacy Directive as a natural experiment: after restrictions on data use, display ad effectiveness (purchase-intent lift) fell by about 65% in the EU relative to other countries. Quantifies the privacy-targeting trade-off.
course_use: Key reading on GDPR/cookie consent and the limits of targeting; very relevant for EU students. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher); SSRN working paper free.

title: Online Display Advertising: Targeting and Obtrusiveness
author_source: Avi Goldfarb & Catherine E. Tucker, Marketing Science 30(3), 389-404, 2011, article
note: Field-experiment data show contextually targeted ads and obtrusive ads each raise purchase intent, but combining them backfires, especially for privacy-sensitive products: more targeting is not always better.
course_use: Discussion case on ad design plus targeting. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Frontiers: How Effective Is Third-Party Consumer Profiling? Evidence from Field Studies
author_source: Nico Neumann, Catherine E. Tucker & Timothy Whitfield, Marketing Science 38(6), 918-926, 2019, article
note: Field tests of 90+ third-party audience segments from 19 data brokers: segment accuracy is often poor (e.g. gender segments correct well under expectations) and lifts over random selection range from roughly 0% to 77%; given the price premium, many third-party audiences are not economical.
course_use: Must-read on programmatic targeting limits; strong numbers for slides. Accepted manuscript open access via MIT DSpace (https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/136617).

title: When Does Retargeting Work? Information Specificity in Online Advertising
author_source: Anja Lambrecht & Catherine Tucker, Journal of Marketing Research 50(5), 561-576, 2013, article
note: Field experiment with a travel site: dynamic (product-specific) retargeting is on average less effective than generic retargeting, except when consumers have already refined their preferences. Behavioural targeting must match the decision stage.
course_use: Use for the behavioural targeting/retargeting session. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher); SSRN version free.

title: Algorithmic Bias? An Empirical Study of Apparent Gender-Based Discrimination in the Display of STEM Career Ads
author_source: Anja Lambrecht & Catherine Tucker, Management Science 65(7), 2966-2981, 2019, article
note: A gender-neutral STEM job ad was shown to fewer women because young women are more expensive to reach in ad auctions: delivered targeting is shaped by platform economics, not only advertiser intent.
course_use: Ethics and limits of algorithmic targeting; discussion on fairness. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher); SSRN version free.

title: An Audience of One: Behaviorally Targeted Ads as Implied Social Labels
author_source: Christopher A. Summers, Robert W. Smith & Rebecca Walker Reczek, Journal of Consumer Research 43(1), 156-178, 2016, article
note: Experiments show behaviourally targeted ads act as social labels that change consumers' self-perception (e.g. 'sophisticated') and raise purchase intent, but only when consumers believe the targeting is accurate.
course_use: Consumer-behaviour angle on targeting; good for discussing experimental designs. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Consumer Privacy Choice in Online Advertising: Who Opts Out and at What Cost to Industry?
author_source: Garrett A. Johnson, Scott K. Shriver & Shaoyin Du, Marketing Science 39(1), 33-51, 2020, article
note: Very few US users opt out of behavioural advertising (about 0.23% of impressions), but opt-out impressions sell at a large discount (about 52% lower price). Quantifies the economic value of behavioural targeting.
course_use: Pair with Goldfarb & Tucker 2011 for a privacy-targeting trade-off session. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher); SSRN version free.

title: Targeting and Privacy in Mobile Advertising
author_source: Omid Rafieian & Hema Yoganarasimhan, Marketing Science 40(2), 193-218, 2021, article
note: Machine-learning targeting framework on large mobile in-app ad data; behavioural information drives most of the gain in click prediction, and the paper shows how platform and advertiser incentives for targeting diverge under privacy rules.
course_use: Advanced reading for analytics-oriented students. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook
author_source: Brett R. Gordon, Florian Zettelmeyer, Neha Bhargava & Dan Chapsky, Marketing Science 38(2), 193-225, 2019, article
note: 15 large RCTs at Facebook: observational methods often badly overstate the lift of targeted ads because targeting selects people already likely to buy. Key lesson on why targeted campaign results look better than they are.
course_use: Discuss targeting effectiveness vs selection bias (link to Sharp's critique). WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Retention Futility: Targeting High-Risk Customers Might Be Ineffective
author_source: Eva Ascarza, Journal of Marketing Research 55(1), 80-98, 2018, article
note: Two field experiments: targeting customers with the highest churn risk is less effective than targeting those with the highest uplift (sensitivity to the intervention). The cleanest teaching example for uplift targeting.
course_use: Central reading for uplift/causal targeting. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher); SSRN version free.

title: Positioning Your Product
author_source: David A. Aaker & J. Gary Shansby, Business Horizons 25(3), 56-62, 1982, article
note: Classic six positioning strategies (by attribute, price/quality, use/application, product user, product class, competitor) plus a step-by-step positioning process including perceptual mapping.
course_use: Core positioning reading for bachelor level; basis for a positioning-strategy exercise. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Three Questions You Need to Ask About Your Brand
author_source: Kevin Lane Keller, Brian Sternthal & Alice Tybout, Harvard Business Review 80(9), 80-86, 2002, article
note: Frame of reference, points of parity and points of difference: the standard framework behind positioning statements; examples of establishing category membership and compelling, believable PODs.
course_use: Core reading; students write a POP/POD positioning statement for a brand. HBR, paid; check WU access via Business Source.

title: Blue Ocean Strategy: From Theory to Practice
author_source: W. Chan Kim & Renee Mauborgne, California Management Review 47(3), 105-121, 2005, article
note: Academic version of the Blue Ocean argument (first in HBR 82(10), 2004): strategy canvas, four-actions framework (eliminate-reduce-raise-create), value innovation. The strategy canvas is a practical positioning visualisation alternative to perceptual maps.
course_use: Workshop: students draw a strategy canvas for an industry. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Customer Intimacy and Other Value Disciplines
author_source: Michael Treacy & Fred Wiersema, Harvard Business Review 71(1), 84-93, 1993, article
note: Three value disciplines (operational excellence, customer intimacy, product leadership): market leaders excel in one and meet threshold levels in the others. Links positioning to the operating model.
course_use: Positioning-strategy framework alongside Porter; HBR, check WU access via Business Source.

title: What Is Strategy?
author_source: Michael E. Porter, Harvard Business Review 74(6), 61-78, 1996, article
note: Distinguishes operational effectiveness from strategic positioning; variety-, needs- and access-based positioning; trade-offs and fit. Connects marketing positioning to the generic strategies.
course_use: Strategic foundation for positioning; HBR, check WU access via Business Source.

title: Meaningful Brands from Meaningless Differentiation: The Dependence on Irrelevant Attributes
author_source: Gregory S. Carpenter, Rashi Glazer & Kent Nakamoto, Journal of Marketing Research 31(3), 339-350, 1994, article
note: Experiments show that differentiation on an irrelevant attribute (e.g. 'flaked coffee crystals') can create a valued brand position; a counter-intuitive and memorable result for positioning discussions.
course_use: Discussion starter on what makes a valid point of difference. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Competitive Positioning and the Resource-Based View of the Firm
author_source: Graham Hooley, Amanda Broderick & Kristian Moller, Journal of Strategic Marketing 6(2), 97-116, 1998, article
note: Links positioning options (price, quality, innovation, service, benefit, tailored offerings) to the firm's marketing resources; positioning typology grounded in the resource-based view.
course_use: Conceptual reading for master-level strategic marketing. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: The Development and Validation of a Scale Measuring Consumer/Customer-Derived Generic Typology of Positioning Strategies
author_source: Charles Blankson & Stavros P. Kalafatis, Journal of Marketing Management 20(1-2), 5-43, 2004, article
note: Consumer-derived typology of eight positioning strategies (e.g. top of the range, service, value for money, reliability, attractiveness, country of origin, brand name, selectivity) with a validated measurement scale.
course_use: Use the scale items in a student survey on brand positioning. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Brand-Positioning Strategies from a Consumer Perspective
author_source: Christoph Fuchs & Adamantios Diamantopoulos, European Journal of Marketing 44(11/12), 1763-1786, 2010, article
note: Vienna-based study comparing concrete-attribute, abstract-attribute, benefit-based and surrogate positioning strategies of real brands; benefit-based positioning tends to be evaluated most favourably. Local (University of Vienna) research.
course_use: Empirical positioning-effectiveness reading. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Customer-Perceived Positioning Effectiveness: Conceptualization, Operationalization, and Implications for New Product Managers
author_source: Christoph Fuchs & Adamantios Diamantopoulos, Journal of Product Innovation Management 29(2), 229-244, 2012, article
note: Defines and measures positioning effectiveness through dimensions such as favourability, dissimilarity (differentiation) and credibility; gives a ready-to-use scale for assessing a product's position.
course_use: Students apply the scale to evaluate a new product's positioning. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Positioning Options for Achieving Brand Association: A Psychological Categorization Framework
author_source: Girish N. Punj & Junyean Moon, Journal of Business Research 55(4), 275-283, 2002, article
note: Categorisation-theory view of positioning: exemplar- vs prototype-based positioning and when to position within or against a category. Theoretical backing for the frame-of-reference concept.
course_use: Theory reading linking consumer psychology to positioning. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: The Impact of Advertising Positioning Strategies on Consumer Price Sensitivity
author_source: Ajay Kalra & Ronald C. Goodstein, Journal of Marketing Research 35(2), 210-224, 1998, article
note: Experiments show that value-oriented vs differentiation-oriented advertising positioning changes willingness to pay and price sensitivity.
course_use: Links positioning decisions to pricing outcomes. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: The Relationship Between Unique Brand Associations, Brand Usage and Brand Performance: Analysis Across Eight Categories
author_source: Jenni Romaniuk & Elise Gaillard, Journal of Marketing Management 23(3-4), 267-284, 2007, article
note: Unique brand associations are rare and mostly held by a brand's own users; questions the value of chasing 'unique' positioning. Data across eight categories.
course_use: Pair with Keller et al. 2002 for a critical discussion of points of difference. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Messung und Gestaltung der Markenpositionierung
author_source: Volker Trommsdorff & Marcel Paulssen, chapter in F.-R. Esch (ed.), Moderne Markenfuehrung, Gabler, pp. 1363 ff., 4th ed. 2005, book chapter (German)
note: German overview of positioning measurement: image differential, factor-analytic positioning model and their assumptions and limits, plus the Wettbewerbs-Image-Struktur-Analyse (WISA) incl. a consideration-set version; illustrated with the premium pilsner market (Beck's).
course_use: German-language reading for the perceptual-mapping session; free PDF on markenlexikon.com.

title: Alternative Perceptual Mapping Techniques: Relative Accuracy and Usefulness
author_source: John R. Hauser & Frank S. Koppelman, Journal of Marketing Research 16(4), 495-506, 1979, article
note: Head-to-head comparison of factor analysis, discriminant analysis and similarity-based MDS for perceptual maps: factor analysis of attribute ratings was the most accurate, easiest to interpret and to use. Classic guidance for choosing a mapping method.
course_use: Methods reading before students build their own maps. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Mine Your Own Business: Market-Structure Surveillance Through Text Mining
author_source: Oded Netzer, Ronen Feldman, Jacob Goldenberg & Moshe Fresko, Marketing Science 31(3), 521-543, 2012, article
note: Mines forum posts (cars, drugs) to derive brand co-mention networks and perceptual maps that match survey-based maps; shows user-generated content as a cheap source for positioning analysis.
course_use: Showcase of text-based perceptual maps; students replicate the idea with reviews. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher); SSRN version free.

title: Mining Marketing Meaning from Online Chatter: Strategic Brand Analysis of Big Data Using Latent Dirichlet Allocation
author_source: Seshadri Tirunillai & Gerard J. Tellis, Journal of Marketing Research 51(4), 463-479, 2014, article
note: LDA on about 350,000 reviews across 15 firms in 5 markets extracts quality dimensions and brand positions over time; perceptual maps by dimension and dynamics of positioning.

title: Automated Marketing Research Using Online Customer Reviews
author_source: Thomas Y. Lee & Eric T. Bradlow, Journal of Marketing Research 48(5), 881-894, 2011, article
note: Extracts product attributes from digital-camera reviews and builds correspondence-analysis maps of brands and attributes; compares results with traditional market research.
course_use: Example of attribute extraction plus a CA map from text. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Mining Brand Perceptions from Twitter Social Networks
author_source: Aron Culotta & Jennifer Cutler, Marketing Science 35(3), 343-362, 2016, article
note: Infers brand perceptions (eco-friendliness, luxury, nutrition) from follower overlap with exemplar accounts on Twitter; correlates highly with survey ratings. Scalable perceptual measure for 200+ brands.
course_use: Example of social-network-based perceptual mapping. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Visualizing Asymmetric Competition Among More Than 1,000 Products Using Big Search Data
author_source: Daniel M. Ringel & Bernd Skiera, Marketing Science 35(3), 511-534, 2016, article
note: Uses consumer search (clickstream) data to produce competitive maps for more than 1,000 TVs, capturing asymmetric competition; shows how big data extend market-structure maps.
course_use: Visual material for competitive-structure analysis. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Frontiers: Determining the Validity of Large Language Models for Automated Perceptual Analysis
author_source: Academic method using general LLMs (ChatGPT, Claude etc.); Marketing Science 43(2)
note: Shows LLM-elicited brand similarity judgments produce perceptual maps that agree closely with survey-based maps. Exercise: prompt an LLM for pairwise brand similarities, run MDS, compare with student-survey map; generate personas from cluster profiles and critique validity and bias.

title: Segment attractiveness scoring and GE/McKinsey-style matrix
author_source: Lyndon Simkin & Sally Dibb, Marketing Intelligence & Planning 16(7), 407-417, 1998 (key reference); portfolio-matrix background in Wind & Mahajan 1981
note: Weighted multi-factor scoring of segments on market attractiveness (size, growth, margins, competitive intensity) vs business strength/fit, plotted in a 3x3 directional-policy matrix to choose undifferentiated, differentiated, concentrated or niche targeting.
course_use: Spreadsheet exercise: score 4-6 segments and plot them. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Multidimensional scaling (MDS) perceptual maps
author_source: Tammo H.A. Bijmolt & Michel Wedel, Journal of Marketing Research 36(2), 277-285, 1999; overview: Paul E. Green, Journal of Marketing 39(1), 24-31, 1975 (doi 10.1177/002224297503900105)
note: Builds maps from overall similarity judgments without pre-specified attributes; Bijmolt & Wedel compare data-collection methods and MDS variants and their effect on map quality and respondent burden.

title: Correspondence analysis for brand-attribute maps
author_source: Donna L. Hoffman & George R. Franke, Journal of Marketing Research 23(3), 213-227, 1986; see also Torres & Bijmolt, European Journal of Operational Research 195(2), 628-640, 2009
note: Maps brands and attributes jointly from pick-any association tables (brand x attribute counts); the cheapest perceptual map from standard brand-tracking data. Torres & Bijmolt add asymmetric brand-to-attribute vs attribute-to-brand associations.

title: Attribute-based perceptual maps via factor analysis / PCA biplots
author_source: K.R. Gabriel, Biometrika 58(3), 453-467, 1971 (biplot); comparison in Hauser & Koppelman, Journal of Marketing Research 16(4), 1979
note: Reduce attribute ratings to two factors and plot brands as points and attributes as vectors (biplot). Hauser & Koppelman found factor-based maps most accurate and interpretable; the standard approach in Lilien & Rangaswamy's Marketing Engineering.
course_use: Default classroom method; students produce a biplot from survey ratings. Paid (Oxford Academic); WU-Lizenz pruefen.

title: Ideal-point and vector models / preference mapping
author_source: Terry Elrod, Marketing Science 7(1), 21-40, 1988; Wayne S. DeSarbo & Jianan Wu, Journal of Marketing Research 38(2), 244-253, 2001
note: Adds consumer preferences to a perceptual space: ideal points (most preferred location) or preference vectors (more is better); Elrod infers such maps from panel choice data. Basis for spotting positioning gaps and segment-specific ideal points (joint space / external preference mapping).
course_use: Shows how segments' ideal points connect targeting and positioning decisions. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Revealed-preference (purchase-data) market-structure maps
author_source: Sebastian Gabel, Daniel Guhl & Daniel Klapper, Journal of Marketing Research 56(4), 557-580, 2019 (P2V-MAP); precursor Steven M. Shugan, Journal of Marketing Research 24(1), 1-18, 1987 (doi 10.1177/002224378702400101)
note: Derives positioning maps from purchase data instead of surveys; P2V-MAP learns product embeddings from shopping baskets and projects them with t-SNE to map large retail assortments.

title: Text-mining / UGC-based perceptual maps
author_source: Sungwoo Moon & Wagner A. Kamakura, International Journal of Research in Marketing 34(1), 265-285, 2017; see also Netzer et al., Marketing Science 31(3), 2012
note: Converts online reviews into brand-attribute or co-occurrence data and then into positioning maps (via CA, MDS or topic models); Moon & Kamakura translate review text directly into a product positioning map.
course_use: Mini-project: collect reviews, count attribute mentions, run CA. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: LLM-based perceptual maps
author_source: Peiyao Li, Noah Castelo, Zsolt Katona & Miklos Sarvary, Marketing Science 43(2), 254-266, 2024; guidelines: Sarstedt, Adler, Rau & Schmitt, Psychology & Marketing 41(6), 1254-1270, 2024 (doi 10.1002/mar.21982)
note: Prompt an LLM for pairwise brand similarities or attribute ratings, then run MDS or factor analysis; validated against human surveys. Sarstedt et al. give guidelines and caveats for using LLM 'silicon samples' in marketing research.

title: Uplift (incremental response) modelling for targeting
author_source: Piotr Rzepakowski & Szymon Jaroszewicz, Knowledge and Information Systems 32(2), 303-327, 2012; application: Ascarza, Journal of Marketing Research 55(1), 2018
note: Models the difference in response between treated and control groups (uplift trees, two-model approach) to target customers who change behaviour because of the campaign rather than those likely to respond anyway.

title: Propensity and lookalike (audience expansion) modelling
author_source: Haishan Liu, David Pardoe, Kun Liu, Manoj Thakur et al., Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD Conference, 165-174, 2016
note: Describes LinkedIn's audience-expansion (lookalike) system: seed audience, similarity and propensity models, and the reach vs precision trade-off; the mechanics behind platform lookalike audiences.

title: Targeting policy evaluation with heterogeneous treatment effects
author_source: Guenter J. Hitsch, Sanjog Misra & Walter W. Zhang, Quantitative Marketing and Economics 22(2), 115-168, 2024
note: Framework to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects (e.g. causal forests) and evaluate the profit of targeting policies with randomised data; shows that good effect prediction does not automatically yield a profitable targeting policy.
course_use: Advanced reading for the analytics track; pairs with uplift modelling. WU-Lizenz prüfen (paid via publisher)

title: Marketing Management (16th ed., Global Edition)
author_source: Philip Kotler, Kevin Lane Keller, Alexander Chernev; Pearson, 16th ed., 2021/2022; textbook
note: Core STP reference: Ch. 6 'Identifying Market Segments and Target Customers' (bases for B2C/B2B segmentation, segment attractiveness, targeting strategies) and Ch. 7 'Crafting a Customer Value Proposition and Positioning' (frame of reference, points of parity/difference, positioning statement). Chernev's value-proposition/positioning logic makes Ch. 7 sharper than earlier editions.
course_use: Lead textbook reading for the STP session(s); paid (approx. EUR 70-90 print, cheaper eText) - WU-Lizenz prüfen (Pearson eLibrary).

title: Principles of Marketing (19th ed., Global Edition)
author_source: Gary Armstrong, Philip Kotler (US ed. with Sridhar Balasubramanian); Pearson, 19th ed., 2023/2024; introductory textbook
note: Ch. 7 'Customer Value-Driven Marketing Strategy: Creating Value for Target Customers' opens Part 3: four-step model (segmentation, targeting, differentiation, positioning), segmentation levels (mass, segment, niche, micromarketing), requirements for effective segmentation, targeting strategies, value-proposition grid ('more for more' etc.), positioning statement. Very student-friendly with many brand examples.
course_use: Bachelor-level foundation reading; paid (approx. EUR 60-80) - WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Marketing-Management: Konzepte - Instrumente - Unternehmensfallstudien (15. Auflage)
author_source: Philip Kotler, Kevin Lane Keller, Marc Oliver Opresnik; Pearson Deutschland (Hallbergmoos), 15. aktualisierte Aufl., 2017, 1012 S.; German textbook edition
note: German adaptation of Kotler & Keller with German-language terminology (Marktsegmentierung, Zielmarktbestimmung, Positionierung) and DACH company cases; segmentation/targeting and positioning chapters mirror Kotler & Keller (check TOC of the edition held). Useful for German-speaking students and exam terminology.
course_use: Alternative German reading to Kotler & Keller; e-version via Pearson eLibrary - WU-Lizenz prüfen; print approx. EUR 60.

title: Marketing: Grundlagen marktorientierter Unternehmensführung - Konzepte, Instrumente, Praxisbeispiele (14. Auflage)
author_source: Heribert Meffert, Christoph Burmann, Manfred Kirchgeorg, Maik Eisenbeiß; Springer Gabler, 14. Aufl., 2024, 877 S.; German standard textbook
note: German standard text; Marktsegmentierung is treated in the Marketingstrategien chapter (13th ed.: section 5.2.3, pp. 334-337: Segmentierungskriterien, Anforderungen an Segmente) together with Marktbearbeitungsstrategien (undifferenziert/differenziert/konzentriert) and Positionierung; the Käuferverhaltens- und Marketingforschung chapter covers the data side. Verify section numbers in the 14th ed.
course_use: German core reading for STP; SpringerLink e-book - WU-Lizenz prüfen (Springer eBook packages usually licensed); print approx. EUR 50.

title: Marketingmanagement: Strategie - Instrumente - Umsetzung - Unternehmensführung (7. Auflage)
author_source: Christian Homburg; Springer Gabler, 7. Aufl., 2020; German textbook (English version: 'Marketing Management: A Contemporary Perspective')
note: Structured along seven perspectives; segmentation, Zielmarktwahl and Positionierung sit in the strategic perspective, with methods (cluster analysis etc.) in the information-related perspective. Strong on methods and B2B segmentation. No 8th edition found as of Oct 2026; check before ordering.
course_use: German reading for students wanting more method depth than Kotler; SpringerLink e-book - WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Market Segmentation: How to Do It and How to Profit from It (revised 4th ed.)
author_source: Malcolm McDonald, Ian Dunbar; Wiley, 4th ed., 2012 (ISBN 978-1-118-43267-9); practitioner handbook
note: Practitioner process: defining the market, market mapping (who buys vs. who decides), micro-segments built from what is bought, where, when and how plus decisive buying motives (DBMs), then clustering micro-segments into segments; many worksheets and B2B examples. Complements the statistical view with a managerial, needs-based procedure.
course_use: Good for group project templates (market map, micro-segment worksheet); paid (approx. EUR 40) - e-book via Wiley/ProQuest, WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind (20th anniversary ed.)
author_source: Al Ries, Jack Trout; McGraw-Hill, orig. 1981, anniversary ed. 2001; trade classic
note: Origin of the positioning concept: owning a word in the prospect's mind, positioning of a leader vs. a follower, repositioning the competition, line-extension trap, the power of the name. Short chapters and famous cases (Avis 'We try harder', 7-Up 'Uncola') ideal for discussion; a counterpoint to evidence-based views (Sharp).
course_use: Short excerpt reading (first chapters plus one case chapter) for the positioning session; paid (approx. EUR 15-20).

title: Obviously Awesome: How to Nail Product Positioning so Customers Get It, Buy It, Love It
author_source: April Dunford; Ambient Press, 2019; practitioner book
note: Modern, step-by-step positioning method especially for B2B/tech: five components (competitive alternatives, unique attributes, value, best-fit target customers, market category) plus relevant trends, and a 10-step team positioning process. Excellent for showing that targeting and positioning are decided together.
course_use: Run the 10-step process as an in-class workshop on a student start-up/product case; paid (approx. EUR 20, also audiobook).

title: Sales Pitch: How to Craft a Story to Stand Out and Win
author_source: April Dunford; Ambient Press, 2023; practitioner book (follow-up to Obviously Awesome)
note: Shows how a positioning is translated into a sales narrative built from eight pitch components (e.g., insight/setup, alternatives, differentiated value, proof, objection handling); bridges positioning to marketing communication and B2B sales.
course_use: Optional reading for the 'positioning to execution' link; paid (approx. EUR 20).

title: Crossing the Chasm (3rd ed.)
author_source: Geoffrey A. Moore; HarperBusiness, 3rd ed., 2014; trade classic (tech marketing)
note: Adoption-lifecycle segmentation (innovators, early adopters, early/late majority, laggards) and beachhead targeting: Ch. 4 'Target the Point of Attack' (target-customer scenarios, niche selection) and Ch. 6 'Define the Battle' (competitive positioning, the widely used positioning-statement template 'For (target customer) who (need)...').
course_use: Excerpt Ch. 4 and 6 for B2B/tech targeting and positioning; paid (approx. EUR 15-20).

title: How Brands Grow: What Marketers Don't Know
author_source: Byron Sharp (Ehrenberg-Bass Institute); Oxford University Press, 2010; evidence-based marketing book (sequel: Romaniuk & Sharp, How Brands Grow Part 2, OUP 2016, rev. 2021)
note: Key critical counterweight to classic STP: evidence that competing brands' customer bases look alike (brands compete as if markets are not segmented), Double Jeopardy, growth via penetration and light buyers, distinctiveness over differentiation, 'sophisticated mass marketing'. Ideal for a debate session 'targeting vs. mass reach'.
course_use: Assign chapters on user profiles and differentiation for a structured debate; paid (approx. EUR 30-40).

title: Building Distinctive Brand Assets
author_source: Jenni Romaniuk (Ehrenberg-Bass Institute); Oxford University Press, 2018; evidence-based marketing book
note: How brands become recognisable via non-verbal cues (colours, logos, characters, shapes) and how to measure asset fame and uniqueness (distinctive asset grid). Complements positioning: what the brand stands for vs. how it is recognised; supports the distinctiveness-vs-differentiation discussion.
course_use: Optional reading for positioning/brand-identity session; paid (approx. EUR 35).

title: The Long and the Short of It: Balancing Short and Long-Term Marketing Strategies
author_source: Les Binet, Peter Field; IPA, 2013; report-style book based on the IPA Effectiveness Databank
note: Evidence from about 1,000 IPA cases: broad-reach brand building vs. narrowly targeted activation (60:40 rule), penetration vs. loyalty objectives, emotional vs. rational campaigns. Directly informs how narrowly to target and the long-term role of positioning.
course_use: Use the summary charts ('10 principles') in class; IPA shop purchase (approx. GBP 50+), summaries widely free.

title: Blue Ocean Strategy (expanded ed.)
author_source: W. Chan Kim, Renée Mauborgne; Harvard Business Review Press, expanded ed., 2015; strategy book
note: Alternative to segment-and-target thinking: chapter 'Reach Beyond Existing Demand' (three tiers of noncustomers, de-segmenting by commonalities), strategy canvas and ERRC grid (eliminate-reduce-raise-create) as a visual positioning tool; cases such as Cirque du Soleil and [yellow tail].
course_use: Use the strategy canvas as an alternative to perceptual maps; paid (approx. EUR 25).

title: Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice
author_source: Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, David S. Duncan; HarperBusiness, 2016; innovation/marketing book
note: Jobs-to-be-done theory as needs/situation-based segmentation (milkshake example): segment by the job customers hire a product for rather than by demographics. Strong discussion piece on choosing segmentation bases.
course_use: Pair early chapters with the Think with Google intent-vs-demographics piece; paid (approx. EUR 20).

title: Strategic Brand Management: Building, Measuring, and Managing Brand Equity (5th ed., Global Edition)
author_source: Kevin Lane Keller, Vanitha Swaminathan; Pearson, 5th ed., 2019/2020; textbook
note: Ch. 2 'Customer-Based Brand Equity and Brand Positioning': competitive frame of reference, points of parity vs. points of difference, desirability/deliverability criteria, brand mantra; the most rigorous textbook treatment of positioning.
course_use: Reading for the positioning session (Ch. 2); paid - WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Strategie und Technik der Markenführung (9. Auflage)
author_source: Franz-Rudolf Esch; Vahlen, 9. Aufl., 2018 (newer edition with Dennis Esch possible); German brand management textbook
note: German reference for Markenpositionierung: separate positioning chapter (5th ed. pp. 152-183, 6th ed. pp. 157-186) within brand identity/brand strategy; positioning models, emotional vs. factual positioning, implementation in communication; many DACH brand cases.
course_use: German reading for positioning/brand sessions; paid (approx. EUR 45) - check WU library (Vahlen eLibrary/beck-online).

title: Principles of Marketing Engineering and Analytics (3rd ed.)
author_source: Gary L. Lilien, Arvind Rangaswamy, Arnaud De Bruyn; DecisionPro Inc., 3rd ed., 2017; analytics textbook with software
note: Dedicated chapters on segmentation and targeting (cluster analysis, discriminant analysis for targeting, profile dashboards) and positioning (perceptual maps, joint-space and preference maps); exercises run in De Bruyn's Enginius cloud software, with cases.
course_use: Basis for a hands-on analytics lab (segmentation + perceptual map); book paid (approx. USD 70), Enginius course licences; verify chapter numbers in the 3rd ed.

title: R for Marketing Research and Analytics (2nd ed.)
author_source: Chris Chapman, Elea McDonnell Feit; Springer (Use R!), 2nd ed., 2019, 492 pp.; analytics textbook
note: Ch. 11 'Segmentation: Clustering and Classification' (pp. 299-340): hierarchical clustering, k-means, model-based clustering (mclust), latent class analysis, naive Bayes and random forests to classify new customers into segments; stresses actionability over statistical fit. Simulated segment dataset; free code and data on the companion site r-marketing.r-forge.r-project.org.
course_use: Code-along lab in R; SpringerLink - WU-Lizenz prüfen; companion code/data free.

title: Python for Marketing Research and Analytics
author_source: Jason S. Schwarz, Chris Chapman, Elea McDonnell Feit; Springer, 2020; analytics textbook
note: Ch. 10 'Segmentation: Unsupervised Clustering Methods for Exploring Subpopulations' (pp. 223-241) and Ch. 11 'Classification' for assigning customers to segments; all analyses as Colab notebooks.
course_use: Python alternative to Chapman & Feit; SpringerLink - WU-Lizenz prüfen; notebooks free.

title: Cutting-Edge Marketing Analytics: Real World Cases and Data Sets for Hands On Learning
author_source: Rajkumar Venkatesan, Paul Farris, Ronald T. Wilcox; Pearson FT Press, 2014 (updated as 'Marketing Analytics: Essential Tools for Data-Driven Decisions', UVA Press, 2021); case-based analytics book
note: Darden case approach: each chapter pairs a technical note with a real company case and dataset; includes cluster-analysis-based segmentation and targeting/resource-allocation cases. Bridges STP theory and data-driven decisions (check TOC for the segmentation chapter number).
course_use: Use one segmentation case + dataset for a graded assignment; paid (approx. EUR 50); O'Reilly access - WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Handbook of Market Segmentation: Strategic Targeting for Business and Technology Firms (3rd ed.)
author_source: Art Weinstein; Routledge (Haworth), 3rd ed., 2004, reissued 2013; practitioner handbook
note: Practical B2B/technology segmentation guide: segmentation research design, bases for business markets, segment evaluation, targeting decisions, implementation checklists; counterpart to consumer-dominated textbook examples.
course_use: B2B segmentation reference for projects; Routledge e-book - WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: Principles of Marketing (OpenStax)
author_source: Maria Gonzalez Albrecht, Mark Green, Linda Hoffman et al.; OpenStax (Rice University), 2023; open textbook, CC BY 4.0
note: Ch. 5 'Market Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning' (from 5.1 Market Segmentation and Consumer Markets through B2B segmentation, targeting strategies, positioning and perceptual maps) with learning objectives, key terms and review questions.
course_use: Free pre-reading or catch-up text for bachelor students; open access (web, PDF).

title: Principles of Marketing (University of Minnesota Libraries open edition)
author_source: Adapted from a 2010 Flat World Knowledge text; University of Minnesota Libraries Publishing, 2015; open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA
note: Ch. 5 'Market Segmenting, Targeting, and Positioning': 5.1 targeted vs. mass marketing, 5.2 how markets are segmented, 5.3 selecting target markets and target-market strategies, 5.4 positioning and repositioning offerings; discussion questions per section.
course_use: Free supplementary reading and question bank; open access.

title: Market Segmentation, Targeting, and Positioning (chapter in Strategic Marketing Management)
author_source: Emmanuel Mogaji; Springer, 2025; textbook chapter
note: Recent concise chapter-length STP overview with current digital/data-driven examples; a single-chapter alternative to long textbook chapters.
course_use: Short reading; SpringerLink - WU-Lizenz prüfen.

title: The value of getting personalization right - or wrong - is multiplying (Next in Personalization 2021 Report)
author_source: Nidhi Arora et al.; McKinsey & Company, Nov 2021; consultancy report/article (approx. 11 pp.)
note: Headline data on the endpoint of targeting (segment of one): 71% of consumers expect personalised interactions, 76% are frustrated without them; companies excelling at personalisation earn 40% more revenue from it; top-quartile personalisation worth over USD 1 trillion in the US. Good for discussing micro-targeting economics.
course_use: Pre-reading for 'from segments to personalisation'; contrast with Gartner 2025 regret data; free.
